summary: WorkOS Applied AI engineer Zack Proser argues that human attention, rather than agent throughput, limits sustainable AI-assisted software development. Using an internal BlogBot bug as an example, he shows how Claude Code, Slack, Linear, and MCP can complete and verify a fix without repeated human intervention. He recommends voice-first parallel workflows, layered lint/build/test and browser-verification gates, continuous improvement from agent conversation histories, and attention to developer well-being, including an Oura Ring MCP integration. Audience questions address early-career skill development, unwieldy JSONL histories, and voice interaction.

title: Your coding agent doesn't always follow your rules
summary: Talha Sheikh of Checkout.com explains why coding agents can claim completion while missing requirements, leaving humans to enforce correctness. He introduces Vector Harness, which uses Claude Code hooks and deterministic checks to verify agent output, and discusses multi-agent workflows, asynchronous checks, LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, code-review feedback loops, and the broader shift toward harness engineering.

title: Your Coding Agent Just Got Cloned And Your Brain Isn't Ready
topics: [{"slug":"developer-workflows-and-testing","name":"Developer workflows and testing"},{"slug":"coding-and-developer-tools","name":"Coding and developer tools"},{"slug":"safety-and-governance","name":"Safety and governance"},{"slug":"rag-context-and-search","name":"RAG, context, and search"}]
summary: Google Labs product manager Rustin Banks presents Jules, an asynchronous coding agent that runs tasks concurrently against GitHub repositories in cloud virtual machines. He contrasts serial programming with orchestrating parallel agents, discusses task generation and downstream review and merging, and demonstrates competing Jest and Playwright implementations alongside conference-app features, accessibility audits, and security audits. He concludes that richer context improves agent performance and identifies Gemini 2.5 Pro as Jules' underlying model at the time of the talk.

title: Your Coding Agent Should Do AI System Engineering

summary: Hugging Face’s Ben Burtenshaw argues that coding agents can extend beyond application programming into AI systems engineering through three increasingly autonomous workflows: writing and distributing CUDA kernels, fine-tuning language models from a prompt, and coordinating multi-agent research experiments. He explains GPU memory bottlenecks and FlashAttention, introduces Hugging Face’s Kernels repository, compares skill-enabled model performance, and describes Git-based experiment management with dashboard and Parquet access.

title: Your Evals Are Meaningless (And Here’s How to Fix Them)
summary: HoneyHive co-founder Mohak Sharma explains why developer-written test sets, generic metrics, and uncalibrated LLM judges can produce evaluation scores that fail to predict real production performance. He recommends domain-expert-defined criteria and edge cases, continuously incorporating problematic production queries into evaluation datasets, and tracking agreement between automated evaluators and human judgments using F1 scores or correlation metrics.

title: Your Finance Agent's Bottleneck Is You

summary: Auditoria AI data scientist Siddanth Emani argues that finance-agent deployments are constrained less by models or hardware than by developers' ability to diagnose production failures and iterate quickly. He proposes parallel subagents isolated in Git worktrees, MCP-connected tools, and an automated workflow spanning Jira tickets, root-cause analysis, test-driven fixes, pull requests, Docker deployments, and QA. A unified interface brings together Kubernetes, Jira, GitHub, and Claude Code while preserving finance controls and positioning humans as verifiers rather than throughput bottlenecks.

title: Your Fine-Tuned Model Is Tech Debt: A 50x ROI House of Cards
summary: Lease End senior data scientist Dan Bjornn describes replacing a retrieval-based customer-intent workflow with a fine-tuned model that reportedly generated $12 million in revenue at 50x ROI, while accumulating operational debt through labeling, synthetic-example generation, retraining, customer-facing classification failures, and vendor lock-in. His team rebuilt around a model-agnostic agentic framework, deployed changes as Markdown files in Amazon S3, accepted higher per-message API costs, and regained flexibility to use providers including OpenAI and Anthropic. He argues that fine-tuning should be a last resort when frontier models cannot solve the problem.

title: Your Insecure MCP Server Won't Survive Production — Tun Shwe, Lenses
topics: [{"slug":"safety-and-governance","name":"Safety and governance"},{"slug":"rag-context-and-search","name":"RAG, context, and search"},{"slug":"evals","name":"Evals"},{"slug":"apis-mcp-and-protocols","name":"APIs, MCP, and protocols"}]
summary: Lenses.io engineers Tun Shwe and Jeremy Frenay explain why enterprise MCP security begins with agent-oriented interface design: reduce exposed tools, constrain inputs with validation, defend tool descriptions against poisoning, and avoid leaking sensitive context. Grounding these risks in OWASP guidance and Lenses’ Kafka-focused open-source MCP server, they contrast local development with production requirements and discuss OAuth authentication, weaknesses of long-lived credentials, and scoped token validation.

title: Your LLM Deception Monitor Is Broken. The Fix Is in the Training Data - Sachin Kumar, LexisNexis
topics: [{"slug":"other-unclassified","name":"Other / unclassified"},{"slug":"observability-and-reliability","name":"Observability and reliability"},{"slug":"architecture","name":"Architecture"},{"slug":"data-and-model-adaptation","name":"Data and model adaptation"},{"slug":"safety-and-governance","name":"Safety and governance"},{"slug":"rag-context-and-search","name":"RAG, context, and search"}]
summary: Sachin Kumar of LexisNexis presents independent research on detecting sleeper-agent backdoors that behavioral evaluations and safety fine-tuning can miss. His approach subtracts base-model activations from fine-tuned-model activations and trains a difference-based sparse autoencoder on that signal. In a controlled, year-triggered SQL-injection experiment using SmolLM2-360M, he reports a 40-fold stronger signal than joint cross-model features, perfect precision, zero false positives, and robustness across middle layers and fine-tuning regimes. He proposes integrating the resulting delta monitor into fine-tuning pipelines while noting that a single feature detects approximately 25% of triggers and that the experiment covered one backdoor type on one 360-million-parameter model.

title: Your LLM Ran Out of Knowledge — Now What?
summary: The talk demonstrates an open-source reasoning framework for applying LLMs in domains with little usable training data, including corporate negotiations and geopolitics. It combines structured scenario parsing, domain-specific heuristics, explicit rules, and realistic constraints; a WorldSim-assisted geopolitical example uses Anthropic and eliminates scenarios that violate prescribed rules while retaining human oversight.

title: Your LLM Stack Is a 2008 Database With Better Marketing
summary: NVIDIA infrastructure engineer Lovina Dmello argues that production ML and LLM breaches usually arise from familiar infrastructure misconfigurations rather than exotic model attacks. Using exposed Ray clusters as an example, she maps threats across model, data, supply-chain, and infrastructure layers; examines the latency and throughput costs of security controls; and recommends authenticated access, least privilege, short-lived credentials, container isolation, network segmentation, and protection of stored data.

title: Your MCP Server is Bad and You Should Feel Bad
summary: Prefect founder and FastMCP creator Jeremiah Lowin explains why MCP servers should be designed as agent-native products rather than exposed REST APIs. He covers focused tool surfaces, agent-centered workflows, orchestration costs, client behavior including Claude Desktop tool caching, pragmatic API bootstrapping, and SEP-1686 asynchronous background tasks.

title: Your Moat Is Your Data Model
summary: Mike Phipps explains why an enterprise AI team's durable advantage lies in modeling its organizational processes and tacit knowledge rather than owning rapidly commoditizing models or interfaces. At the Gates Foundation, the Strategic Intelligence Platform uses a cross-system semantic knowledge graph to support agentic workflows, represent funding and management hierarchies, connect siloed operational data, and enforce governance practices including PII masking. The official session description identifies Neo4j, an MCP server, Claude integrations, and retrieval evaluations as additional elements of the architecture.

title: Your Personal Open-Source Humanoid Robot for $8,999 — Jingxiang "JX" Mo, K-Scale Labs
summary: K-Scale Labs founding engineer Jingxiang "JX" Mo presents K-Bot, an approximately $9,000 open-source humanoid, alongside the smaller Z-Bot. He describes openly available hardware and software, modular upgrades, VR teleoperation, Python/Rust development tools, reinforcement-learning locomotion and manipulation, simulation with Isaac Sim or MJX, and support for vision-language and vision-language-action models. The recording concludes with audience questions about practical applications, trade-offs, and competing humanoid prices.

title: Your realtime AI is ngmi — Sean DuBois (OpenAI), Kwindla Hultman Kramer (Daily)
summary: OpenAI's Sean DuBois and Daily's Kwindla Hultman Kramer explain why voice-AI systems should be designed around low-latency networking, emphasizing conversational response times near 500 milliseconds, end-to-end voice-to-voice latency, and WebRTC's advantages over WebSockets for streaming audio. They discuss the OpenAI Realtime API, Pion, and Pipecat; demonstrate Squabbert, a Raspberry Pi-based voice agent using MLX Whisper and Gemma 3; and include a community project introduction.

title: Your Support Team Should Ship Code
topics: [{"slug":"developer-workflows-and-testing","name":"Developer workflows and testing"},{"slug":"leadership","name":"Leadership"},{"slug":"apis-mcp-and-protocols","name":"APIs, MCP, and protocols"},{"slug":"coding-and-developer-tools","name":"Coding and developer tools"}]
summary: Zapier product leader Lisa Orr explains how constantly changing third-party APIs create integration failures and support backlogs, and how support staff can help ship fixes under engineering review. After discovery revealed that gathering documentation, logs, and bug context was a major bottleneck, the team built LLM-assisted diagnosis and testing tools; its standalone Autocode playground struggled because it interrupted existing workflows. Adoption improved by embedding Diagnosis into Zapier and Jira workflows, using MCP alongside tools such as Cursor, and orchestrating the Scout project through Zaps so completed merge requests reach support for validation.

title: Your Voice Agent Doesn't Need a Frontier Model
summary: Joel Allou and Ornella Bahidika present Ace, an AI voice tutor designed around an approximately 950-millisecond response budget. Instead of relying on a frontier model, deterministic state machines handle lesson progression, student knowledge, and turn-by-turn context while Claude Haiku 4.5 generates speech. A comparison against Claude Opus 4.7 reports roughly 900-millisecond responses for the scaffolded smaller model, with strict structural guardrails needed to control drift.

title: ACP: The Universal Remote Control for AI Agents — Alex Hancock, Block
summary: Alex Hancock proposes the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) as a standard interface between client applications and agent harnesses. He explains its messaging and extension mechanisms, demonstrates different clients using Goose, and describes remote transport as a way to place clients, harnesses, tools, and models independently. He argues that interoperability could encourage a client ecosystem with better user experiences.

title: I Monitored Crime Audio. Voice Agents Scare Me More. — Sumanyu Sharma, Hamming AI
summary: Sumanyu Sharma argues that voice-agent failures can spread widely because centralized prompts and architectures affect many users. Drawing on crime-audio monitoring and a failed appointment booking, he recommends a continuous cycle of discovering failures, prioritizing their frequency and severity, testing fixes, checking regressions, and monitoring production. He also warns about adversarial callers and recommends ongoing red teaming.

title: Agents Without Code: Skills, YAML, and Filesystems Replaced Python — Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
summary: Philipp Schmid demonstrates three versions of a GitHub pull request review agent: a manual Python loop, a framework-based implementation, and a hosted agent configured through files and a sandbox. He argues that general tools and skill files can reduce custom orchestration, while developers retain responsibility for domain instructions, workflows, and evaluations.

title: The unreasonable effectiveness of BM25 for agentic search — Jo Kristian Bergum, Hornet.dev
summary: Jo Kristian Bergum argues that BM25 is becoming more useful for agentic search because the user has changed: language models bring general knowledge, generate specific queries and iteratively refine searches. He defines agentic search as retrieval within an agent loop, requiring a capable model, a harness and an efficient retrieval engine. Using BrowseComp+, he describes high answer accuracy when evidence is supplied directly and lower accuracy when models must retrieve it, arguing that evidence acquisition is the bottleneck in that setting. He cautions that unsuitable BM25 parameters for long documents can make lexical baselines look weaker than they are. Exact matching, cost and inspectable results motivate combining BM25 with file-system workspaces, progressive disclosure and tools such as grep. He advocates evaluating completed tasks rather than relying solely on single-query ranking metrics, and presents a claimed Hornet efficiency advantage over anonymized engines on 100 million web documents.

title: Your company brain will leak secrets: how we stopped it for big banks — Tanmai Gopal, PromptQL
summary: Tanmai Gopal presents an approach to securing a company brain used by coding agents. He proposes a companywide wiki with per-file access scopes, human approval and attribution for knowledge changes, and access checks using the requesting user's permissions. For collaborative agents, he describes keeping credentials outside the sandbox and injecting user credentials when tools access data.

title: Mousepower: agents that can’t be measured, can’t be managed. — Maximillian Piras, Yutori
summary: Maximillian Piras argues that agent adoption requires understandable measures of value and practical ways to verify results. He proposes tracing token spend to outcomes and choosing tasks with moderately uncertain execution steps but clear acceptance criteria. “Mousepower” is a conceptual analogy for communicating agent efficiency, rather than a defined metric.

title: AI-Generated Code Is Already Competing With Human Code — Daksh Gupta, Greptile
summary: Daksh Gupta presents Greptile's observational analysis of agent-written and human-written pull requests. He reports similar results across revert rates, PR-size comparisons, flagged issue severity and review rounds, with differences in failure patterns. He argues that rising code volume requires validation focused on user contracts, future risks and author intent, supported by codebase analysis and sandboxed browser agents.

title: MCP Apps: Give the Model Data, Give the User a UI — Dustin Mihalik, Indeed
summary: Dustin Mihalik describes lessons from building job-search MCP apps at Indeed. Widgets provide controlled links and job details, but can obscure information from the model or discourage further searches. He recommends sharing displayed data and user interactions with the model, explaining UI behavior in tool descriptions, and separating search tools from rendering tools so the model can explore and filter results before displaying them.

title: Agents Are Where Microservices Were in 2015 — Roberto Milev & Uday Kanagala, Navan
summary: Roberto Milev and Uday Kanagala describe lessons from operating agents at Navan. Comparing agent infrastructure to early microservices, they recommend establishing a reliable single agentic loop before adding orchestration complexity. Their approach combines persistent runtime sessions, memory, progressively loaded skills, tool-call tracing, trajectory evaluations, and fine-grained authorization. They identify cost control, replay, debugging, and emerging standards as unresolved challenges.

title: Long-Horizon Agents Need Experiments, Not Just Prompts — Erina Karati
summary: Erina Karati describes how Project Paradox’s game agents lost source attribution, uncertainty and planning consistency over longer interactions. She presents an autoresearch loop that evaluates controlled scenarios, collects traces and tests small policy changes against a balanced scorecard. The talk reports an improved mango-rumor example while explicitly withholding claims of general improvement without repeated results.

title: The Search Engine for the Agentic Web — Will Bryk, Exa
summary: In this talk attributed by recording metadata and the supplied organizer record to Will Bryk, Exa is presented as a search engine designed for AI agents. Bryk forecasts that machine-issued searches will exceed human searches in 2026 and eventually outnumber them by a thousandfold. He contrasts recommendation-oriented search with precise, database-like retrieval and argues that reliable information is essential infrastructure for understanding and coordination. He describes Exa's founding thought experiment: use a language model to judge every query-document pair, then reduce the prohibitive cost through techniques including precomputed embeddings and combinations with keywords. He recounts launching the consumer search engine Metaphor in 2022 and pivoting toward an API after repeated requests for programmatic access. Capabilities described include complex research queries, a claimed 200-millisecond search endpoint, selective token extraction, structured results and configurable search constraints. Exa Connect extends retrieval to a marketplace of private data providers, illustrated with Similarweb information. The closing vision is aspirational: make each search feel like a year of research completed in a second. Forecasts, performance comparisons and product capabilities are the speaker's claims, rather than independently verified findings.

title: Tribal Dungeons of Global Shipping: AI Agents at Global Scale — Dmitry Buykin, Maersk
summary: Dmitry Buykin describes turning shipping operations knowledge into procedures agents can execute safely. He emphasizes explicit process definitions, bounded execution, shared traces, expert feedback, and repeated executable corrections. The central argument is that reliability comes from the refinement system surrounding agents and the accumulated procedure corpus.

title: KV Cache-Aware Routing and P/D Disaggregation on Kubernetes — Yuchen Fama & Ashish Kamra, Red Hat
summary: Yuchen Fama and Ashish Kamra explain KV cache-aware routing and prefill/decode disaggregation for agentic inference. They demonstrate faster responses through cache reuse, describe how separating prefill from decode can reduce streaming latency, and discuss workload and network conditions that determine whether disaggregation helps. An ongoing H200 case study illustrates reported gains and the need for workload-specific tuning.

title: Building GTM AI Agents: Lessons from Deploying to 6,000 Users — Sait Izmit, Snowflake
summary: Sait Izmit describes lessons from deploying Snowflake’s internal go-to-market assistant to roughly 6,000 users. He reports more than a million questions answered and emphasizes answer quality, phased rollout, and sustained adoption work. He also describes expanding from data questions into workflow automation, adapting the architecture as requirements change, and using conversation logs to identify product and sales-enablement gaps.

title: Why LLM Recommenders Will Be AI's Biggest Consumer App — Devansh Tandon, Meta
summary: Devansh Tandon argues that recommendation systems follow scaling curves similar to LLMs and could become a major consumer application of AI. He outlines traditional, LLM-inspired, LLM-native, and agentic recommendation paradigms, then describes building recommenders through semantic content IDs, language-and-catalog training, and recommendation post-training. He presents steerable feeds and lower inference costs per hour of engagement as reasons for their potential.

title: Vertical Mobility: Inference from MVP to Trillion-Parameter Workloads — Sitanshu Gupta, CoreWeave
Autoresearch Made Our Models 3x Faster — Tejas Bhakta, Morph
summary: Tejas Bhakta explains how his team uses autoresearch to tune custom GPU kernels around human-provided optimization ideas. He emphasizes correctness checks, hardware and model context, and end-to-end benchmarking to detect reward hacking. He reports a combined threefold speedup from kernel and hardware optimizations, while warning that roughly 80% of attempts are bad.

title: One Designer + AI. Hundreds of Deliverables. — Vincent Wendy, AI Engineer
summary: The speaker describes using AI tools and reusable design systems to handle conference design as the only designer. His approach combines explicit design specifications, automated graphics and signage workflows, visual checks, and rapid handling of schedule changes.

title: The Missing Layer in Agentic AI — Giedrius Šteimantas, Oxylabs
summary: Giedrius Šteimantas describes rebuilding a shopping agent around web-access infrastructure. He recommends search APIs for discovery, validated scraper output for product evaluation, and browser automation for checkout. His central argument is that validating content before sending it to a model and limiting browser use can reduce wasted tokens and improve reliability.

title: AI in GTM at Notion — Flora Liu
summary: Flora Liu describes Notion's work to unify fragmented go-to-market systems around shared customer context and a know, decide, act, and learn loop. Humans and agents use the same data, while agents research and draft and sales representatives retain approval and customer relationships. The presentation covers customer profiles, signal-driven Temporal workflows, outcome feedback, and early reported improvements.

title: Generative UI... in Python? — Jeremiah Lowin, Prefect
summary: Jeremiah Lowin presents Prefab, a Python framework for composing interactive interfaces delivered through MCP apps. He explains its focus on enterprise information workflows, its serializable UI representation, and examples ranging from interactive tables to direct file uploads and agent-generated interfaces.

title: Pinecone 2.0 — Edo Liberty, Pinecone
topics: [{"slug":"theory-of-mind","name":"Theory of mind"},{"slug":"tribal-knowledge","name":"Tribal knowledge"},{"slug":"rag-and-knowledge","name":"RAG and knowledge systems"},{"slug":"knowledge-freshness","name":"Knowledge freshness"},{"slug":"nexus-manifests-and-contexts","name":"Nexus manifests and contexts"},{"slug":"knowledge-curation","name":"Knowledge curation"},{"slug":"noql","name":"NoQL"},{"slug":"coding-agents","name":"Coding agents"},{"slug":"agent-efficiency","name":"Agent efficiency"}]
summary: In “Pinecone 2.0,” metadata identifies Edo Liberty as the speaker. He uses theory of mind and a Yahoo Answers anecdote to explain why users overestimate what systems know. He distinguishes general model knowledge, specific private information retrievable from documents, and tribal knowledge synthesized across company processes, priorities and decisions. Enterprise agents, he argues, resemble brilliant new hires who start each session without organizational understanding. He proposes a shared knowledge layer that persists, specializes by domain, supports expert ownership and keeps facts current despite obsolete documents. He presents Pinecone Nexus through connectors, contexts, tasks and queries. A manifest specifies relevant tasks, entities and information; Nexus manages semantic maps, Markdown notes, SQL tables, vector indexes and graph structures. Import and curation assimilate new information, while NoQL lets agents specify query budgets and receive structured grounded output. A runtime coding agent writes, executes and revises code at query time, producing reusable code for the task. Liberty reports a tooling-prompt reduction from roughly 150,000 tokens to fewer than 1,000, alongside early-access token and speed improvements and qualitative accuracy gains. These are speaker-reported results without detailed evaluation methodology in the supplied transcript. He closes by announcing public preview for “tomorrow,” which does not independently establish a calendar launch date.

title: The Building Blocks of GTM Orchestration — Arman Vaziri, Ramp
summary: Arman Vaziri describes Ramp’s foundations for go-to-market automation: an internal customer data platform, durable agent execution, searchable unstructured information, and customizable skills. Pre-meeting briefs illustrate how solving one team’s workflow creates reusable capabilities. The broader goal is to turn campaign intent into coordinated channel outputs with human review.

title: Every step you take, every call you make: the reliable agent stack — Giselle van Dongen, Restate
summary: Giselle van Dongen presents Restate as an infrastructure layer for long-running agents. A Slack research-agent demo illustrates journal-based recovery, durable human-approval waits, isolated session state, updates to ongoing runs, and cancellation. The talk also describes shared LLM gateways and an event-driven distributed-log architecture.

title: The Agentic Commerce Stack — Ahnaf Prio, Best Buy
summary: Ahnaf Prio explains agentic commerce from a merchant perspective, covering standardized product data, agent communication, checkout, and payment authorization. A fictional bakery agent demonstrates the flow. He emphasizes behavioral evaluations, protocol compliance, and latency testing while distinguishing existing integrations from still-developing autonomous shopping capabilities.

title: Your Agreements Are a Database You Can't Query — Hiral Shah, Docusign & Sean Sodha, NVIDIA
topics: [{"slug":"enterprise-agreement-data","name":"Enterprise agreement data"},{"slug":"nemotron-parse","name":"Nemotron Parse"},{"slug":"contract-table-extraction","name":"Contract table extraction"},{"slug":"rag-context-and-search","name":"RAG, context, and search"},{"slug":"agreement-manager","name":"Agreement Manager"},{"slug":"extraction-throughput","name":"Extraction throughput"},{"slug":"hybrid-ocr-pipelines","name":"Hybrid OCR pipelines"},{"slug":"quantization-and-decoding","name":"Quantization and decoding"}]
summary: Hiral Shah and Sean Sodha describe Docusign and NVIDIA's work to make enterprise agreements structured and queryable, especially the pricing tables that generic extraction can flatten incorrectly. Shah reports processing about one million agreements daily and cites a Deloitte study estimating $2 trillion in negotiated value that organizations fail to recover. The presenters describe Nemotron parse as an approximately 850–900 million-parameter vision language extractor that returns text, layout, reading order and preserved table structure in a single pass, with NVIDIA NIM or vLLM serving options. An Agreement Manager demo illustrates order-form upload, metadata and pricing extraction, CSV export and API access; Docusign also describes an organization-wide agreement data model and search. Shah reports roughly 20× greater table-extraction throughput than the other open-source models they tested, without supplying full comparison conditions in the transcript. The Q&A clarifies that Docusign retains a hybrid pipeline with OCR for other fields and clause text. The speakers distinguish bulk preprocessing from low-latency document Q&A and discuss future retrieval, agent, quantization and multi-token-generation work.

title: The Spatial Harness: Bringing Agents to the Canvas — Max Drake, tldraw
summary: Max Drake presents a progression of canvas-agent experiments: interpreting screenshots and structured canvas data, autonomously navigating and editing a canvas, coordinating visible agents, managing coding agents through a dependency graph, and scripting a desktop editor. He argues that a shared canvas can make collaboration with agents and their working states easier to understand.

title: Tokens Should Have Jobs — Katelyn Lesse & Angela Jiang, Anthropic
summary: Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang propose allocating agent tokens to distinct jobs: execution, advising, grading, and reflection into memory. They report financial-analysis experiments in which these strategies produce different results under a fixed token budget. They argue that strategy choice should reflect the cost of obtaining a fully correct answer and the desired reliability, and describe combining these roles through agent orchestration.

title: Which AI startups actually land enterprise contracts? — Brian Lewis, Millennium
summary: Speaking personally, Brian Lewis describes why enterprise AI purchases fail across product value, security, reliability and legal requirements. He argues that vendors need working integrations, credible operational controls and enforceable data commitments, while buyers must improve architecture, entitlements and change management to benefit from AI.

title: Large clusters for small models — Daniel Svonava, Superlinked
No Memory, No Harness: Why the Database Is the Last Line of Defense — Kay Malcolm, Oracle
summary: Kay Malcolm describes how faster AI-assisted coding left her distributed team without shared decision context. She presents memory as an essential component of an agent harness and argues for consolidating different memory representations in a database. She describes a team memory broker using Oracle's agent memory SDK to share context associated with forks, branches, and commits while developers retain control.

title: Why Your AI Agent Needs a Wallet: USDC and Nanopayments — Harshal Bhangale, Circle
summary: Harshal Bhangale argues that payment barriers limit agents' ability to access resources and complete tasks. He compares two agents planning a World Cup trip: the agent without a funded wallet drafts an email and cannot call, while the wallet-equipped agent pays providers, sends an email, and delivers a phone briefing. He presents wallet spending limits and Circle's nanopayments architecture as ways to support autonomous, frequent, small payments.

title: Distill the LLM, Don't Serve It: Search & Personalization at DoorDash — Raghav Saboo, DoorDash
summary: Raghav Saboo presents DoorDash's approach to improving marketplace discovery through semantic understanding of items and shopper intent. He describes generating relevance supervision offline, representing catalogs with semantic IDs, building reusable consumer memory and generating personalized collections. The central pattern is to distill expensive LLM reasoning into representations and smaller models that existing retrieval and ranking systems can serve efficiently.

title: Give the Agent a Budget, Not a Token — Sachin Malhotra, Anthropic
summary: Sachin Malhotra argues for bounding agent autonomy with operational budgets. Drawing on an accidental workload deletion incident and CI examples, he describes asymmetric permissions, replenishing rate limits, aggregate monitoring, and an undo test. Prompts explain intent, while infrastructure enforces limits and supplies trusted agent identity.

title: How We Built an Agent That Improves Itself — Zubin Aysola, Weights & Biases
summary: Zubin Aysola describes how the team evaluates and improves ARIA using production traces, offline simulations, and comparisons between agent variants. The demo turns a production trace into a regression task, identifies incorrect SDK usage, and tests a targeted prompt or skill change. He emphasizes reliable measurement and continued human judgment.

title: Build-Time vs. Run-Time: Why Dev Tools Fail in Production — Averi Kitsch & Prerna Kakkar, Google
summary: The speakers distinguish flexible database tools for developer assistance from constrained tools for production agents. They describe destructive actions and prompt-driven data leaks, then explain how predefined SQL, restricted access and application-controlled identity parameters can limit agent privileges. They also recommend clear tool descriptions, separate read and write tools, actionable errors and simple inputs.

title: x402 isn’t good (yet) — Jan Curn, Apify
summary: Jan Curn discusses Apify’s experience implementing x402 for agent payments. He argues that payment verification before blockchain settlement exposes sellers to double spending, while fixed payments and conflicting HTTP requirements complicate longer-running tools and MCP integration. He describes upfront charging with refunds, considers batch settlement promising, and presents a markdown interface through which agents can purchase prepaid tokens for existing APIs and MCP tools.

title: How Software Factories Improve Themselves — Suraj Gupta, Warp
summary: Suraj Gupta presents three ways software factories can improve over time: updating agent skills from run feedback, retaining facts in persistent memory, and routing tasks to suitable models. Warp demonstrations illustrate human-reviewed skill changes, traceable memories, and configurable routing. He also describes internal routing evaluations and planned customer-facing evaluation tools.

title: From VLM/VLA's to Embodied Agents — Armen Aghajanyan, Perceptron AI
summary: Armen Aghajanyan presents an approach to embodied foundation models that combines perception, reasoning, and control. He discusses sparse video supervision, learned perceptive objectives, and token routing to reduce visual context costs. Examples include agentic object detection, robotic video annotation, and book sorting. He reports a tradeoff between video pretraining and teleoperation data, while acknowledging unresolved temporal understanding and robustness limitations.

title: Why AI Agents Need Million-Token Context — Thomas Wolf & Olive Song, MiniMax
summary: Thomas Wolf interviews Olive Song about MiniMax M3’s combination of coding, multimodal understanding and a million-token context window. Song explains the motivation for longer agent context, the sparse-attention design and training with text and vision from the first step. She also discusses internal research projects, community feedback and agent harnesses that she says are helping develop M3.1.

title: Coding Agents Don't Scale Themselves. Neither Do Your Teams. — Patrick Debois, Tessl
summary: Patrick Debois argues that scaling coding agents requires organizational change alongside technical improvements. He advocates shared context and harnesses, team rituals focused on recurring agent failures, accountable platform ownership, and measuring human intervention and reuse. He also discusses hiring, cost optimization, and choosing levels of autonomy according to risk.

title: Building ambitious software — Jonathan Kelley, Dioxus Labs & Cognition
summary: Jonathan Kelley describes how the Dioxus team adopted coding agents while maintaining a demanding quality bar for its Rust app framework. He reports benefits in platform integration, debugging, and release maintenance, but continued difficulty with meaningful tests. His central argument is that faster code generation increases the importance of architecture, clear intent, and careful code review.

title: Teaching LLMs to Speak Spotify — Yves Raimond & Jacqueline Wood, Spotify
summary: Yves Raimond and Jacqueline Wood explain Spotify's shift toward language-steerable personalization. They describe catalog semantic IDs, NEO's staged training recipe, reported recommendation and decoding results, and evaluation with LLM judges grounded in listening history and behavioral signals.

title: Operating Distributed Inference Systems at Scale — Nishant Gupta & Naman Ahuja, Meta
Orchestras, Not Factories: How the Fastest Builders Work — Charlie Holtz, Conductor
summary: Charlie Holtz presents principles for working with coding agents: experiment with new tools, limit workflow optimization to specific needs, protect important areas with human review, supply organizational context, and use persistent cloud sandboxes. He demonstrates collaborative Conductor workspaces and remotely initiated tasks, then argues for humans directing teams of people and agents like an orchestra.

title: Two Bugs That Hid in Plain Sight: A vLLM Debugging Detective Story — Asaf Gardin & Yuval Belfer
The Signal Layer: What to Build When Anything Can Be Built — Lena Hall, Akamai
summary: Lena Hall argues that widely available AI shifts competitive value toward choosing worthwhile problems and communicating their value accurately. Her proposed “signal layer” preserves a product’s specific purpose through content creation and organizational handoffs. She recommends grounding decisions in direct experience and customer relationships, keeping limitations attached to claims, and testing what audiences actually understand.

title: FinOps for AI Agents: Who Spent All the Tokens? — Tisha Chawla & Susheem Koul, Microsoft
summary: Tisha Chawla and Susheem Koul present Token Ops, a system for attributing agent spending and applying budget policies during execution. They describe instrumentation, a ledger, and developer-authorized controls that steer agent behavior before resorting to termination. Their demonstration covers preview mode, budget halts, and instructions encouraging shorter outputs. They report lower spending and higher run completion in their benchmarks.

title: Realtime Voice Agents with Frontier Intelligence — Bohan Li, EliseAI
summary: Bohan Li explains techniques for reducing latency in a cascaded voice-agent system while using slower language models. The presentation covers speculative transcription, early response generation with background tool calls, and cached speech prefixes combined with newly synthesized audio. A recorded clinic-booking demonstration is followed by closing remarks about EliseAI's housing and healthcare focus, expansion in the Bay Area, and recruiting.

title: Building the Engine While Flying the Plane: Launching the Figma MCP Server — Jesse Lumarie, Figma
summary: Jesse Lumarie describes how a one-day-a-week experiment became Figma’s first MCP server in about three months. The talk covers design-context representation, automated evaluations, reuse of existing code components, workarounds for uneven MCP client support, and the decision to launch locally before building a remote server.

title: From Scratch to SOTA: Training a 3B State-Space Vision Model — Krishna Prasad Srinivasan, Sarvam
summary: Krishna Prasad Srinivasan describes Sarvam's three-billion-parameter document vision-language model for English and 22 Indian languages. He explains its state-space backbone, block-level OCR with layout and reading-order harnesses, four-stage training curriculum, and emphasis on data generation, evaluation, and verifiable OCR rewards. He reports benchmark results and enterprise digitization deployments, then discusses synthetic data, extraction fidelity, an intended public Indic benchmark, and control over data use.

title: Are LLM Performance Benchmarks Reliable? — Ashok Chandrasekar & Jason Kramberger, Google
From Tokenmaxxing to Trusted Throughput — Mingsheng Hong, Ironclad
summary: Mingsheng Hong describes Ironclad's approach to improving AI coding spend through trusted throughput: output validated by automated checks, human judgment, and customer experience. He discusses measuring value alongside cost, evolving productivity metrics, improving review and CI, and controlling waste through budgets, bounded agent loops, prompt caching, and context management.

title: Tolan: Voice-First AI Companion — Paula Dozsa, Tolan
summary: Paula Dozsa describes engineering Tolan's voice-first AI companion around fast responses, interruptions and changing conversational context. She explains per-turn model routing, retrieval-based memory and context reconstruction, then describes the team's use of coding, review and evaluation agents.

title: How We Solved Agent Building — Andrew Qu, Vercel
summary: Andrew Qu describes successive versions of Vercel's internal data science agent, moving from a large SQL-generation prompt through scoped agent chains to a single agent managing its own state. He reports that a sandboxed file system approach improved evaluations, while skills distilled from recurring queries supplied reusable context. He presents the framework called Eve in the supplied sources and argues for agents built around specific company knowledge.

title: Stop Chunking Like It's 2022 — Yuval Belfer, AI21 Labs

summary: Yuval Belfer argues that effective chunk size depends on the query, making a single indexing-time choice a source of retrieval loss. Small chunks preserve focused details but lose broader context; large chunks retain context while diluting specific information. Experiments indexing datasets at six sizes, contrasting Seinfeld questions, and an answer-informed oracle illustrate this tradeoff. Belfer reports an oracle gap of roughly 20–40 percent, without specifying whether that means relative improvement or percentage points. His practical approach indexes multiple window sizes, queries every index, maps retrieved chunks to whole documents, and combines document rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. He reports matching or beating the best fixed-size approach across QMSum, NarrativeQA, Seinfeld, and FinanceBench. The stated tradeoff is roughly two to five times the memory, with little added latency from parallel retrieval and inexpensive fusion. Selecting the number and sizes of windows and improving fusion remain open research questions.

title: You’re Not Thinking Big Enough: Rebuilding Food Systems with AI Agents — Cody Menefee, Firecrawl
summary: Cody Menefee proposes using an LLM to help farmers choose grazing locations from animal positions, pasture observations, and environmental conditions. He describes labor and daily decision-making as barriers to rotational grazing, and identifies a grazing knowledge base, pasture vision measurements, and open collar APIs as remaining requirements. His closing proposal keeps humans able to confirm or reject model suggestions.

title: How to avoid disaster when vibe-coding a billing engine — Andrew Garvin, Stripe
summary: Andrew Garvin demonstrates using Stripe Projects and a Metronome billing agent to create a sandbox modeled on Lovable’s pricing. He advocates portable skills files, clear errors, realistic test usage and human review before production. He also distinguishes agents as products, buyers and users, explaining how each role affects software pricing and integration.

title: How to Get Your Org to Adopt Coding Agents (Without Shipping Garbage) — Eyal Blum, Figma
summary: The speaker describes Figma's ongoing adoption of coding agents and the technical and cultural friction it creates. He recommends investing in verification, writing detailed plans with independently validated phases, involving skeptical engineers in safety improvements, distinguishing human writing from generated communication, and introducing agents within familiar workflows.

title: No, That's Not a Software Factory — Ryan Cooke, WorkOS
summary: Ryan Cooke describes WorkOS’s effort to embed product planning, project tracking and support triage into its software factory. He argues for measuring customer delivery and reliability rather than code or pull-request volume. The approach combines TARS, Horizon, a PM agent and an internal MCP gateway, with human review throughout planning and execution.

title: Your agents lack context: Here's how to fix "You're absolutely right!" — Brandon Waselnuk, Unblocked
summary: Brandon Waselnuk argues that coding agents need organizational context to produce useful, mergeable code. He describes limitations of curated markdown and MCP access alone, outlines six context-engine capabilities, reports a comparison of runs with and without context, and introduces tools for mapping engineering relationships, checking repository rules and querying relational data.

title: We Let Claude Code and Codex Race Human Researchers — Elie Bakouch, Prime Intellect
summary: Elie Bakouch presents experiments using coding agents to improve results on the Optimizer Speedrun. He reports that Claude Code and Codex surpassed the human record, but their gains combined existing methods rather than introducing novel optimizers. He discusses differences in persistence, token use and literature search, then outlines a more controlled benchmark and a discovery loop involving evaluation, human judgment and larger-scale testing.

title: It’s Tokens All The Way Down: How RLMs are Different — Kevin Madura, AlixPartners
summary: Kevin Madura explains recursive language models as models that manipulate input as variables in a REPL and can delegate subtasks to other models. He argues that this approach reduces pressure on the main context window and suits large, decomposable tasks. He illustrates it with numerical extraction, cohort retention analysis, invoice consolidation, log analysis, harness optimization and code security reporting.

title: Reverse-Engineering the AI Buyer — Aliisa Rosenthal, Acrew Capital
summary: Aliisa Rosenthal draws on her experience at OpenAI to explain how AI companies can reduce friction in enterprise sales. She recommends starting with self-service and automation, adding people at demonstrated bottlenecks, limiting resource-intensive pilots, and lowering barriers to adoption. In Q&A, she distinguishes these scaling practices from the hands-on work needed with initial design partners.

title: 500 Skills, Zero Fine-Tuning: LinkedIn's Playbook for AI Agents — Ajay Prakash, LinkedIn
summary: Ajay Prakash describes LinkedIn's infrastructure for giving coding agents internal context through MCP tools and task-specific playbooks. He explains why tool access alone was insufficient, how modular playbooks supply instructions progressively, and how three meta tools support discovery and execution across a large catalog. He emphasizes reliability, shared infrastructure and keeping playbooks current through proposed repository changes.

title: Deep dive on LLM Inference at Scale — Harshul Jain, Audible & Tanmay Sah, Independent AI Researcher
summary: This workshop explains LLM inference bottlenecks through attention, GPU memory, KV caching, and the prefill and decode phases. It covers model quantization and attention variants, then serving optimizations and workload-specific comparisons of vLLM and SGLang.

title: Agent Frameworks Considered Harmful — Rémi Louf, .txt
summary: Rémi Louf describes how an attempt to automate his morning workflow developed into a small event-driven agent runtime. Early failures—duplicate briefs, a lost voice note, and untracked prompt changes—led him to add a durable event log, attempt-aware queues, and content-addressed prompt storage. He argues that agents can be simple declarative files subscribing to typed events, while the runtime supplies scheduling, isolation, traceability, replay, and strict boundaries for tool calls and inter-agent communication.

title: I Gave an AI a Body — Cyrus Clarke, MIT Media Lab
summary: Cyrus Clarke, introduced in the recording as an MIT Media Lab researcher, describes connecting an OpenClaw agent to a 900-pin shape display and inviting it to explore physical expression rather than execute productivity tasks. He reports that its early movements resembled breathing, explored the grid’s boundaries and spelled a greeting. He treats these encounters as provocative design experiments, not evidence of consciousness. The first video reportedly reached 15 million views and drew reactions ranging from admiration to demands that he stop. Clarke places the work alongside his plant-data project Data Garden and The Anemoia Device, which transforms images into scents, and explains influences from object-oriented ontology, sensory aesthetics or aisthesis, and nature. He chose a display without a face, limbs or obvious human affordances to explore non-anthropomorphic embodiment. Initial interactions suffered from human-pleasing responses, delays of roughly 45 seconds to two minutes, and missing memory. He describes a closed loop that generates gesture candidates, checks their legibility, scores them, incorporates human validation and stores accepted expressions. After several weeks, he reports approximately 32 useful gestures and nearly immediate nods for yes-or-no questions, with physical responses preceding verbal ones. His developing thesis, Aesthetic Machines, argues for sensory, expressive physical AI that people can understand and experience as welcoming. The recording’s loop name, rendered as Pneuma Lab, remains unresolved against the supplied written sources’ BODYLAB terminology.

title: Voice Agents Can Just Do Things — Charlie Guo, OpenAI
summary: Charlie Guo argues that voice agents can respond through actions and visual feedback as well as speech. He describes three combinable interaction modes—speech to speech, speech to action, and event to speech—and emphasizes using existing application tools, supporting accessibility, and choosing communication methods around the user's context.

title: How Anthropic Builds: Lessons from Labs — Mike Krieger, Anthropic
summary: Mike Krieger describes how he delegates broader goals to Claude and how Anthropic Labs organizes rapid experiments. He discusses a weekend code migration, shared agent workflows, human comprehension as a code-review bottleneck, and two-week project reviews. The interview also covers product integration, opportunities for specialized startups, and maintaining perspective and openness under pressure.

title: Building uReview, Uber’s Multi-Agent Code Review Engine — Will Bond & Ameya Ketkar, Uber
summary: Will Bond and Ameya Ketkar describe Uber’s uReview code review system, its routing and comment filtering architecture, and how developer feedback and agent trajectories helped improve quality and cost. They explain team-specific reviewers, report adoption and addressal metrics, and discuss preserving human feedback as agents take on more implementation and review work.

title: Scale the Judgment, Not the Model — Andrew Orobator, Reddit
summary: Andrew Orobator argues that reliable coding agents depend on explicit engineering judgment, verification and human oversight. He describes skills, work logs and personas as ways to preserve that judgment, illustrates the approach with a feature-flag cleanup agent, and discusses enforcing safeguards and maintaining guidance as code changes.

title: The Best Models Still Reason Like Toddlers — Andrew Dai, Elorian
summary: Andrew Dai argues that frontier models often substitute pattern recognition for detailed visual reasoning, leading to counting, spatial grounding, and video state-tracking errors. He questions whether common benchmarks capture these weaknesses and describes an approach combining specialized data, synthetic training, architectural changes, and visual chain of thought. He presents robotics, construction safety, and mechanical design as potential applications.

title: Agents' next frontier: agent-to-agent and network effects — Jean-Denis Greze, Town
summary: Greze reframes agent-to-agent collaboration as a search problem: getting the right information into an LLM's context before an answer or tool call. He compares five approaches to crossing information silos under privacy constraints, favors AI-maintained shared knowledge for near-term benefits, and discusses automated disclosure policies, failure modes, and potential collaboration across companies.

title: Inside 847 Production Clinical AI Notes — Sebastian Fox, Composo
summary: Sebastian Fox examines harmful additions, changes, and omissions in AI-generated clinical notes and argues that static evaluation rubrics struggle to judge which differences matter. He proposes continuously discovering failures from real outputs, capturing expert reasoning and corrections, and retrieving relevant examples and references for each evaluation. He reports better performance from this approach on the dataset presented.

title: Physical AI's Next Bottleneck Is Finding the Right Video — Rafael Levi, Bright Data
summary: Rafael Levi argues that finding relevant training video is a bottleneck for robotics and world models. He discusses limitations of staged recordings, simulation, and teleoperation, then presents Bright Data's approach to searching indexed web videos for specific actions before collecting clips. Demonstrations cover dishwashing and clothes folding, with additional proposed uses in driving data and brand discovery.

title: Agentic Sites: Building Hyper Personalized Websites — Carlos Sanchez, Adobe
summary: Carlos Sanchez presents websites that adapt selected content blocks to visitors’ browsing signals and queries. He describes grounding generation in existing site content, evaluating models for accuracy and latency, and letting marketers define personas. Demonstrations cover personalized coffee recommendations and conference comparisons.

title: Get Out of the Model's Way — Kevin Hou, Google DeepMind

summary: Kevin Hou presents Antigravity’s product philosophy of “scaling with intelligence”: as models improve, the product should expose their growing capabilities. He traces the shift from autocomplete and chat to agents, agent managers, and agent teams, using terminal access, Windsurf’s removal of chat, and Antigravity 2.0’s separation of the IDE from the agent manager as examples of difficult product decisions. He describes Gemini 3.5 Flash leading dynamically configured specialist subagents through /teamwork, with generated interfaces for task status and results. Hou reports that an OS-kernel project running Doom used 93 subagents over 12 hours, roughly 15,000 requests and two billion tokens, costing under $1,000. In an internal evaluation-analysis example, he says researchers automated 90% of the workflow: an agent compares control and experiment results, proposes 100 hypotheses, investigates them with parallel subagents, and produces an interactive report. He identifies dynamic subagents, long-lived sidecars listening for external triggers, and inline generative UI as the three central primitives, arguing that builders should choose capabilities that benefit from future model improvements.

title: Robotics Has Been Stuck for 70 Years — Deepak Pathak, Skild AI
summary: Deepak Pathak argues that robotics needs a general-purpose brain and scalable, diverse training data. He describes Skild's approach of sharing one model across robot bodies, combining simulation and human-video pre-training with teleoperation post-training and deployment feedback. He presents manipulation, cooking, locomotion, assembly, delivery, and adaptation demonstrations as examples of this approach.

title: Can LLMs Write Fast Multi-GPU Kernels? — Simran Arora, Together AI
summary: Simran Arora explains how communication between GPUs constrains AI workloads and presents ParallelKittens primitives for writing efficient multi-GPU kernels. She then introduces ParallelKernelBench, an 87-problem evaluation, reporting that tested models produce some useful kernels but struggle with communication ordering, data partitioning, scheduling, and transfer mechanisms. More samples and an agent harness improve correctness, while performance gains plateau.

title: How AI Agents Let GTM Teams Scale — Justin Joyce, Cloudflare
summary: Justin Joyce describes Cloudflare’s approach to supporting go-to-market teams through reusable analytical skills, proactively delivered insights, and a self-service agent workspace. He explains a three-agent reporting workflow and emphasizes curated business knowledge, human review, and feedback. Quoting, approvals, and CRM updates remain areas under development.

title: Homa: The End of TCP for AI Clusters — John Ousterhout, Stanford

summary: John Ousterhout argues that AI inference and agentic workloads increasingly depend on small coordination exchanges, making tail latency important alongside bulk throughput. A single slow synchronization exchange can stall distributed computation and leave GPUs idle. He attributes delays to incast queues, lagging sender-driven congestion control, and byte-stream head-of-line blocking. He presents Homa, a Stanford-developed transport using independent RPC messages, shortest remaining processing time, receiver-issued packet grants, and switch priority queues to favor short messages. In the sample mixed-message benchmark he describes, Homa delivers roughly 13× lower short-message P99 latency than TCP and nearly 2× better latency for the longest messages. These are reported benchmark results, rather than demonstrated end-to-end AI application speedups. At the time of the talk, he says a Linux kernel module is available on GitHub and upstreaming is in progress, and invites developers to experiment with Homa.

title: Multimodal Collaborative Agents for Next-Gen Commerce — Nidhi Kaushik Vyas, Google DeepMind
summary: Nidhi Kaushik Vyas presents a discovery–research–response loop for shopping agents handling unclear user intent. Using a living-room redesign example, she explains how agents can assemble constraints from conversation and images, prioritize useful questions, elicit preferences visually, and adapt response formats. She also describes evaluation at each stage and discusses merchant ontologies and potential agent buyers.

title: How do you diffuse AI into the real world? — Varun Shenoy, Long Lake
summary: Varun Shenoy discusses deploying AI in services businesses through Long Lake's experience as an owner and operator. He argues that useful adoption requires progressively earned autonomy, evaluations grounded in actual work, and close collaboration with employees. He connects agent improvement with user adoption and emphasizes integrating tools into existing workflows and learning from people in person.

title: Teaching agents to pay — Anna Spysz, Stripe
summary: Anna Spysz demonstrates a headphone-shopping agent to explain merchant discovery, commerce protocols, agent behavior, and payments. She describes making a merchant catalog accessible through structured data, changes a pushy agent persona to a patient mentor, and walks through a purchase using shared payment tokens. The talk emphasizes user control, spending limits, disclosure, and audit logs.

title: Tethered: Our Agents Are Us — Shu Fang, Two Sigma
summary: Shu Fang describes Two Sigma's approach to running remote cloud agents under employees' own identities. He explains why separate agent accounts proved cumbersome, how existing Kubernetes infrastructure supports this approach, and how attribution headers and controlled web access address its risks. He presents these controls as preserving agent usefulness while reducing risk.

title: When AI Agents Pay and Sellers Monetize: Building x402 Apps on AWS — Anil Nadiminti, AWS
summary: Anil Nadiminti explains how agents could pay for content and APIs through x402, then presents AWS capabilities for buyers and sellers. He describes AgentCore Payments with wallet integration, spending limits, protected keys, and a payment path separated from the agent loop. On the seller side, he describes detecting and verifying bots at the edge and pricing access by content path, bot identity, and request intent.

title: How to Generate Mergeable Code with a Context Engine — Peter Werry, Unblocked
summary: Peter Werry argues that coding agents need task-specific organizational context, including past decisions, team conventions, and architecture rationale. He demonstrates Unblocked generating sourced explanations and supporting planning, code review, and debugging, then introduces tools for querying pull-request history and mapping engineering expertise.

title: Robot Demos Are Easy. Reliability Is Hard — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
summary: Jason Ma explains Dyna Robotics' approach to making generalist robot policies reliable for commercial tasks. He describes broad pre-training, task-specific fine-tuning, and reward models that identify mistakes for targeted recovery-data collection. He reports 99.4% napkin-folding success over 24 hours and discusses deployments and generalization to new sites.

title: Software Engineering Is Becoming Factory Engineering — Zach Lloyd, Warp

summary: Zach Lloyd introduces himself as Warp's founder and a former Google principal engineer who led engineering on Google Docs. He argues that software engineering is moving from interactive coding agents toward automated software factories, with engineers increasingly designing and managing the systems that build products. His proposed loop combines agent triage, specifications, implementation, review, verification and monitoring with human checkpoints. He says Warp's move to open source supported a public factory and ecosystem, while automation helped manage noisy issues, poor pull requests and verification work. For harder tasks, he recommends separate product and technical specifications; for review and verification, he describes agent-first code review, human intervention based on risk, computer-use checks and continued CI/CD. The underlying architecture includes work intake, a control plane, cloud sandboxes, agent harnesses and a data plane for memory and improvement. Observer agents can improve skills using failures and human corrections, while efficiency should be measured through software shipped, human time and token costs. He introduces an unnamed starter repository and advises organizations to focus on their core products while tuning factory skills to their domains. In Q&A, he emphasizes adaptability, critical thinking, systems understanding and human product taste as essential to building useful software.

title: Weight Folding, CUDA Streams, and the Bug That Made My Model Speak Backwards — Filip Makraduli
Building the Document Context Layer for AI Agents — Jerry Liu, LlamaIndex
summary: Jerry Liu frames modern RAG as an agent harness plus a context layer. He describes a document platform built around parsing, semantic storage, and repeatable workflows, focusing on the difficulty of converting document formats into useful agent context. He discusses hybrid parsing, ParseBench, and a fast initial parsing pass followed by selective visual inspection.

title: The Death of Developer Advocates — Stephanie Jarmak, Sourcegraph
summary: Stephanie Jarmak argues that developer relations must serve agents as both tool users and recommenders while retaining its human audience. She describes evaluating agent tool use through benchmarks and traces, measuring product recommendations across different prompts, and improving documentation, discoverability, and adoption. Her central claim is that reducing friction for agents can also help human developers.

title: Loophole: Adversarial Agents To Stress Test Your Morality — Brendan Rappazzo, Morgan Stanley
summary: Brendan Rappazzo presents Loophole, his personal open source project for testing moral principles with adversarial agents. It translates user-written morals into a formal code, generates cases exposing loopholes or overreach, and either patches the code or asks the user to resolve ambiguity. He also describes experimental applications to chatbot rules, contracts, and simulated legislative voting.

title: If we want them to do Knowledge Work, design them as Knowledge Agents — Benjamin Clavié, Mixedbread

summary: Benjamin Clavié argues that agents doing knowledge work should follow established knowledge-worker patterns. Coding is an unusually tractable subset: identifiers and file paths provide durable search cues, and users often supply narrow tickets. Non-code work instead requires interpreting ambiguous information, reconstructing intent, and determining contextual applicability. He describes tools and specialized roles as a reinforcing loop, where better retrieval enables new workflows and more knowledge production. In the leaderboard he calls Brass Compass, he reports that optimizing retrieval improves accuracy and that a leading configuration reaches 90.2% with 20% fewer tool calls. In the PDF benchmark he calls MatQA, he argues that lexical retrieval limits even human performance, while multimodal search raises the ceiling. Delegating research to searcher agents that return short memos adds a reported 3.5 accuracy points, which he characterizes as roughly a 40% reduction in the remaining oracle gap. His recommendations are to learn from human knowledge organizations, improve tools when performance ceilings appear, train agents to use different search primitives, and orchestrate research around finite context.

title: Rebuilding the web for agents — Liad Yosef, MCP Apps
