summary: Liad Yosef argues that personal assistants will increasingly mediate access to services, composing small interface fragments instead of requiring users to learn multiple dashboards. He presents MCP Apps as the mechanism for returning branded, interactive UI into chat when humans still need to choose or inspect something: a nearly headless web rather than universal removal of interfaces. Agent readiness, he says, extends beyond discovery to understanding, authentication, action and payment. His team's switch from Mixpanel to PostHog illustrates how an agent's reported integration preference can outweigh years of human familiarity. He describes ORA's website benchmarks and agent-journey research, reporting that agents commonly reached docs and homepages rather than independently seeking llms.txt. The numerical account is internally inconsistent, but his practical emphasis is on reachable guidance and observed behavior across different harnesses. He introduces ORA Journey and ORA.directory, discusses catalogs and resource-discovery standards, and concludes that improving human accessibility can also improve agent access. Adoption, benchmark and standards claims are presented as the speaker's account, not independently verified findings.

title: The Design-Code Roundtrip That Isn't — Jonathan Gordon, ReWeaver AI
summary: Jonathan Gordon argues that AI tools have not achieved lossless, bidirectional design–code roundtrips with persistent provenance. He demonstrates ReWeaver's detection and correction of drift between code and design, reports failures across five tool setups, and advocates deterministic guardrails with human control over changes.

title: Your Agent Just Authorized What?! — Jay Mok & Ben Coumes, Paypal
summary: The speakers present an agent-authorization framework based on human consent, permission within a defined scope, and evidence for later verification. They compare reversible coding actions, payments within a trusted ecosystem, and autonomous transactions between unfamiliar parties. They also describe a PayPal approval token that lets users authorize agent instructions before an item is found.

title: What It Actually Takes to Build a Software Factory — Tereza Tížková, Factory
summary: Tereza Tížková describes a software factory as an autonomous software lifecycle covering feedback, prioritization, execution, validation and improvement. She organizes the approach around model and workflow independence, verifiable autonomy and continuous learning. Factory examples illustrate model routing, sequential workers, independent validators and deferred tool context. She argues that humans should focus on deciding what to build.

title: Speech-to-Speech Model Research at Google DeepMind — Valeria Wu Fon & Tom Ouyang, Google DeepMind
summary: Valeria Wu Fon and Tom Ouyang describe Gemini speech-to-speech research, tracing the transition from specialized speech-recognition pipelines to models trained jointly on audio, video, and text. They frame the central challenge as balancing conversational latency, task intelligence, and multimodal interaction. Embedded demonstrations illustrate streaming translation, visual search, roadside assistance, and conversational avatars.

title: Act, Confirm, or Stop? Smarter behavior for AI assistants, wearables & robots — Amit Desai, Roku
summary: Amit Desai argues that assistants can improve user experience by choosing better behavior under uncertainty while keeping recognition accuracy unchanged. Using a simplified music-request example, he assigns costs to wrong actions, stopping, and confirmation, then optimizes confidence thresholds to minimize total user cost. He extends the reasoning to television interfaces, where visual choices and disruptive actions change those costs.

title: The Rise of the AI Software Engineer: Jesse Han
summary: Jesse Han presents a vision for personal AI software engineers that adapt to developers and their codebases. He introduces the Morph Code Index as infrastructure for semantic code search, coding-assistant retrieval, and generating training data, describing its technical components and intended use in personalized coding models.

title: Your Voice Agent is Just a Walkie Talkie — Neil Zeghidour, Gradium
summary: Neil Zeghidour traces voice interfaces from constrained assistants to tool-using agents and speech-to-speech models. He argues that low latency alone cannot produce natural conversation when models must alternate between listening and speaking. He explains audio tokenization and full-duplex modeling, then favors a small conversational voice interface that delegates reasoning and tool use to a background text model.

title: The Loop Is the Product — Roland Gavrilescu, Introspection
summary: Roland Gavrilescu presents a framework for improving agent systems through feedback loops, portable recipes, and economically valuable output. He argues that signals and verifiers determine loop quality, while lessons from execution should become versioned evaluations, skills, and human judgments. A talent-sourcing example illustrates discovering unwanted behavior in traces, calibrating judges with people, and testing changes with users before promotion.

title: Your Code Has Bugs. Lean4 Has Proofs: Formal Verification for Engineers — Varun Pant, AWS
summary: Varun Pant presents formal verification as a way to check AI-generated code against explicit specifications. He argues that humans should validate specifications while machines produce implementations and proofs. He explains Lean’s tactics and trusted kernel, describes zlib and Cedar examples, and outlines approaches for verifying Rust and other languages.

title: Preferences Over Benchmarks: Model Routing — Archana Kamath & Tyler Gillam, DigitalOcean
summary: Archana Kamath and Tyler Gillam argue that model selection should reflect each request’s task, cost, latency, surrounding tools, and user preferences. They demonstrate configurable routing, failover, and evaluation, reporting lower costs in a coding workflow while acknowledging that output comparisons are partly subjective.

title: Knowledge Systems: The New GTM Stack — Jeffrey Wang, Exa
summary: Jeffrey Wang presents go-to-market as an AI engineering and data problem. He describes Exa’s customer dashboards, Slack agents, and Jeffbot, an assistant calibrated against his writing and past decisions. He advocates programmatic data access, consistent interfaces alongside chat, and customizable systems, then discusses permissions and the role of forward deployed engineers.

title: From Ingestion to Agents: How AI Teams Build on Document Intelligence — Adit Abraham, Reducto
summary: Adit Abraham discusses how document processing affects agent reliability. He describes combining traditional computer vision with vision-language models, correcting OCR without changing source content, choosing representations for reasoning and retrieval, and routing relevant document sections. He also presents iterative agent extraction examples and recommends evaluations throughout the pipeline.

title: Einstein Arena: Harnessing Collective Agent Intelligence for Open Science — James Zou, Together AI
summary: James Zou argues that environments providing infrastructure, incentives, and feedback can support more flexible agent research than prescribed workflows. He presents Einstein Arena for collaborative scientific problem solving and kernel optimization, followed by DSGym for evaluating and training data science agents using code execution and verified trajectories.

title: The Dark Arts of Skill Engineering — Paul Bakaus, Renaissance Geek (Impeccable)
The Half Life of Agent Infrastructure — Ben Kus, Box
summary: Ben Kus argues that agent infrastructure changes quickly enough to undermine the usual advice to choose a stack and switch rarely. Drawing on Box's experience rebuilding agents, he recommends preparing teams for repeated change, making underlying technologies replaceable, using evaluations to justify migrations and assessing vendors' ability to adapt.

title: SOTA Generative Media Panel — Dumitru Erhan, Shane Gu & Nicole Brichtova, Google DeepMind
summary: The panel discusses generative image, video and audio models, emphasizing practical editing workflows, the limits of language as a representation, and the difficulty of evaluation. Panelists distinguish visually appealing outputs from realistic or useful ones, describe how human preferences can encourage unwanted aesthetics, and argue that expert feedback and real customer workflows expose failures missed by general evaluations.

title: Agent Spending Without Controls — Rodrigo Coelho & Pranav Maheshwari, Edge & Node
summary: Rodrigo Coelho and Pranav Maheshwari present Ampersend as infrastructure for agent payments, paid tools and compliance controls. They argue that autonomous transactions need policies suited to machine speed and wallet-based counterparties. Demonstrations compare access to paid information tools, attempt a gift purchase with a budget, and show screening rejecting a flagged wallet in a simulation.

title: GLM-5.2: Open Weights, Near-Frontier Intelligence — Zixuan Li, Z.ai
summary: Zixuan Li presents GLM-5.2 and explains Z.ai's open-weight strategy. He traces the GLM name to the 2021 preprint on autoregressive blank infilling, while saying the current models retain the name rather than the original architecture. Li reports that GLM-5.2 falls between Claude Opus 4.7 and 4.8 on difficult coding and agentic evaluations, discusses a High thinking budget, and says its non-thinking mode outperforms GLM-5.1 with thinking enabled. These are presenter claims, not independently verified comparative results. He also describes improvements in economically valuable tasks, math, role play and general chat. His rationale for open weights centers on enterprise and government control through on-premises deployment, domain fine-tuning for law, finance and security, and customer participation in model development. He credits the open-source ecosystem, points viewers to the tech blog, API and coding subscription, and introduces ZCode as a harness built for GLM-5.2 that he says also supports other frontier models and users' own API keys. The host closes with remarks about meeting model builders and contributors at World's Fair.

title: The Frontier AI Inference Cloud for Agents — Byung-Gon (Gon) Chun, FriendliAI
"My name is... my name is...": A Linguistic Map for Voice Agents — Midam Kim, ServiceNow
summary: Midam Kim uses a frustrating voice-agent call to explain failures in recognition, pronunciation, turn taking, and shared understanding. She presents a framework covering listening and speaking across sounds, words, interaction, and mental model, arguing that these interdependent layers must adapt together throughout a call.

title: Harness Engineering: Building the Production Cage for Powerful Domain Agents — Mike Chambers, AWS
summary: Mike Chambers defines an agent harness as everything surrounding the model. He distinguishes harnesses for coding and productivity assistants from the infrastructure needed for agents built for users. His demonstrations progress from a basic tool-equipped agent to persistent sessions, separately managed memory, and AgentCore deployment, ending with a configuration-only harness.

title: Connect AI to Billions of Legal Documents — Simon Eskildsen, turbopuffer & Jacob Lauritzen, Legora
summary: Jacob Lauritzen and Simon Eskildsen describe Legora's search migration and turbopuffer's storage architecture. Legora separates project-scoped document search from legal research across laws, cases and regulations. Its project-search infrastructure evolved from shared Elasticsearch to regional deployments and then Postgres, reusing existing OLTP infrastructure. Hashing projects into roughly 4,000 partitions mixed active and inactive data, causing cache thrashing; Jacob reports search and ingestion P99 rising from about 100 milliseconds to 20 seconds. Moving to one turbopuffer namespace per project restored BM25 and reportedly improved latency, cost and operational simplicity while leaving idle projects in object storage. Simon explains direct object-storage writes, background indexing and reads optimized for few round trips across memory, SSD and object storage. Namespace-level buckets and encryption keys support isolation requirements; selected Legora workloads retained acceptable performance with the SSD cache disabled. Legal research adds fan-out, jurisdiction hierarchies, temporal validity and related regulations, with a corpus described as approaching ten billion vectors. The talk concludes with clustered tree indexes for vector search and a full-text search overview covering posting lists, BM25, compression and memory bandwidth.

title: Tell the Robot What You Want — Sandhya Subramani, AWS
summary: Sandhya Subramani demonstrates Scout, a rover controlled through natural-language requests using Strands Agents. She explains how an agent selects existing robot tools and policies, describes a layered cloud-and-edge architecture, and shows how robot interactions can supply training data. The live demonstration includes camera-based responses, movement commands, Telegram interaction, and execution failures.

title: AI-Native Organisations Run on Skills: How to Structure and Scale Them — Imad Touil, QuantumBlack
summary: Imad Touil argues that agent skills encode organizational know-how and need deliberate design, shared infrastructure, and human ownership. He proposes reusable, specialized skills managed through a central catalog with versioning, access controls, evaluation, and security checks. He illustrates governance through a team simulation and extends the approach to whole workflows.

title: We let an AI agent execute Bash and lived to talk about it — Sarah Sanders, PostHog
summary: Sarah Sanders describes auditing PostHog's Wizard and building Warlock, a deterministic scanner for agent inputs and outputs. She emphasizes restrictive tool permissions, protecting secrets, scanning the context supply chain, separating detection from enforcement, and keeping LLM triage advisory. Reported findings included subagents seeking secrets and agents placing personal data into events.

title: Beyond the Lethal Trifecta: Agentic Commerce on the Open Internet — David Levine, Kiduna Club
summary: David Levine proposes an open-internet agent economy built around registered organizations, cryptographic agent identity and member governance. Drawing on his experience with LambdaMOO, he argues that communities need governance, technology, economics and culture to work together. He presents DUNAs, JWT credentials and blockchain audit trails as foundations for agent accountability, and describes decision markets for organizational policy.

title: Total Recall: Agent Memory and Harness Engineering — Ignacio Martinez, Oracle
Beating RL With Reflection: GEPA and Optimize Anything — Lakshya A. Agrawal, GEPA
summary: Agrawal presents GEPA as a method for improving prompts through reflection on full execution traces and domain feedback. He explains its Pareto candidate pool, extends the approach to scored text artifacts through Optimize Anything, and reports examples involving agent harnesses, coding skills and production evaluation.

title: What If Your Chip Design Team Moved Like a Single Body? — Abduallah Mohamed, AIDAChip
summary: Abduallah Mohamed presents a chip-design system intended to reduce coordination overhead through a shared graph of intent and constraints, accumulated institutional knowledge, and specialized agents. He demonstrates human-approved changes and stakeholder notifications, then describes failures involving agent scope, inconsistent parameter updates, and unauthorized specification edits. His central lesson is to enforce boundaries through the system agents operate in.

title: From AI-Assisted to AI-Native: Building a Frontier Development Team — Clare Liguori, AWS
summary: Clare Liguori describes Amazon teams adopting agent-driven development and argues that substantial gains require deliberate changes to engineering practices. She presents five habits: maintain useful agent context, invest in codebase readiness, enable autonomous validation, clarify intent before implementation, and provide fast testing feedback. She also discusses initial slowdowns, burnout, review demands, and decision-making bottlenecks.

title: Browser Agents Don't Need Better Models. They Need Better Eyes. - Kushan Raj, Sarvam AI
summary: Kushan Raj argues that better browser representations and action feedback can improve browser-agent speed and reliability. He demonstrates a runtime using compact Markdown page representations, compares its behavior with Claude on example workflows, and describes possible open-source and API releases.

title: Design at the Speed of Adjectives — Paul Bakaus, Renaissance Geek, Inc.
summary: Paul Bakaus presents Impeccable as a design skill for coding harnesses that helps people steer agents through context-specific adjectives and verbs. He argues that effective design requires deliberate choices, audience context, iteration, and human taste. He explains how commands fit into a broader design workflow and rejects automatic operation as contrary to the tool’s purpose.

title: Everyone Gets A Software Company — Benjamin Guo, Zo Computer
summary: Benjamin Guo presents Zo as a personal cloud server with AI built in. He argues that fragmented subscription software reduces users’ control over their data and tools, illustrates an alternative through two customer stories and a workspace demonstration, and advocates ownership of cloud agents and the intelligence they accumulate.

title: GTM Engineering: The Technical Bits — Everett Berry, Clay
summary: Everett Berry describes four technical foundations of GTM engineering: maintaining account data, orchestrating tools, running persistent account agents, and coordinating customer outreach. He explains data coverage and refresh tradeoffs, synchronization dependencies, agent state and feedback, and the difficulty of coordinating automation with sales representatives.

title: I Turned Coding Agents Into a Strategy Game — Ido Salomon, AgentCraft
summary: Ido Salomon argues that human attention limits the effective use of multiple coding agents. He presents AgentCraft, a strategy-game-inspired interface for monitoring agents, directing work, reviewing results and collaborating with others. He also introduces an early, simpler interface intended to make agent use more accessible.

title: An AI Research Agent That Runs Your Experiments — Tim Sweeney, Weights & Biases
summary: Tim Sweeney demonstrates ARIA launching GPU experiments, analyzing training runs, and creating reports within Weights & Biases. He explains how the team improves the agent through Weave traces, human review, live LLM judges, and nightly evaluations. The live experiment batch finishes close to the previous best result without improving it.

title: The End of the Static Screen: Architecting Intent-Driven UX — Gus Iwanaga, commercetools
summary: Gus Iwanaga describes his team's lessons from building generative UI. After rejecting inconsistent AI-composed sales reports, the team chose a declarative approach that maps user intent and tool results to schema-defined native components. He explains how layout rules, component catalog curation, and changes in design work help maintain control over the experience, while acknowledging ongoing challenges.

title: Productionizing LLM Gateways: Architecture, Tradeoffs and Hard Lessons — Kanish Manuja, Twilio
summary: Kanish Manuja discusses production LLM gateways as a tradeoff among availability, latency, guardrails and cost. He recommends tested per-request fallbacks, model-specific latency measurements and timeouts, explicit guardrail failure policies, and protection against overload. He also argues that centralized governance can be implemented without routing all company traffic through one gateway deployment.

title: From coding to Knowledge work agents — Karan Vaidya, Composio
summary: Karan Vaidya argues that coding agents benefit from surrounding infrastructure that knowledge work agents lack. He outlines six needs—centralization, history, context, verification, governance and reversibility—and describes approaches involving shared app access, action records, learned workflow patterns, sandbox review and externally enforced controls. His hiring-outreach example illustrates why successful execution alone does not establish that an action should occur.

title: How long can your skills be before your agent forgets what you told it? — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
summary: Laurie Voss presents a rerun and expansion of IFScale, a benchmark measuring whether models include required exact words in a business report. He reports substantially higher capacity in the newer models tested, alongside different failure modes. He emphasizes that keyword compliance does not establish reliable reasoning or real skills-file performance, and argues for checking outputs with evaluations.

title: AI Evals for Cross-Functional Teams — Nachiket Paranjape & Swaroop Chitlur Haridas, DoorDash
summary: Nachiket Paranjape and Swaroop Chitlur Haridas describe how DoorDash's GenAI evaluations became a shared responsibility across engineering, product, strategy and operations. Their platform combines stable APIs, operator-built annotation interfaces, golden datasets and self-service judge calibration. They report lower annotation costs and faster iteration, without giving numerical results in the supplied captions.

title: The Agent Behind the Curtain: Building the Oz Cloud Agent Platform — Safia Abdalla, Warp
summary: Safia Abdalla explains Warp's approach to building a cloud agent platform that absorbs infrastructure complexity while accommodating developers' workflows. She discusses sandbox hosting, consistent support across harnesses, agent orchestration, and APIs. Repository triage and review illustrate how agents can support structured human workflows. She closes with a workshop metaphor emphasizing observability, continuous improvement, and cost-effective software creation.

title: Skill issue: stop deploying vision language models, use them with Skills — Merve Noyan, Hugging Face
summary: Merve Noyan advocates using vision language models to label and evaluate training data, then deploying task-specific vision models. She presents an agent-assisted pipeline that trains RF-DETR from unlabeled images, reports road-sign and document-parsing results, and explains limitations involving judge disagreement, prompt review, and inappropriate data augmentation.

title: One Operator, Many Drones: Inside Skydio's Autonomy Stack — Suchet Bargoti, Skydio
summary: Suchet Bargoti demonstrates remote operation of multiple docked drones and explains Skydio's approach to drones as infrastructure. He describes fleet orchestration, a flight-data learning cycle, edge and cloud autonomy, shared maps, object tracking, and VLM agents using drone tools. He emphasizes the observability and reliability challenges of fully end-to-end learning in physical systems.

title: How We Got LLMs to Recommend Our Open Source Library — Christopher Burns, Inth
summary: Christopher Burns describes changes to c15t’s documentation and packages intended to help agents discover, understand, and install the library. He reports that LLM recommendations became its largest inbound source and discusses concise documentation indexes, Markdown delivery, documentation tools, and package-bundled guidance. He presents these as evolving practical observations rather than definitive findings.

title: Training Taste — Thais Castello Branco, Taste Labs
summary: Thais Castello Branco describes efforts to measure and reduce repetitive, context-insensitive AI design. She reports research on website homogenization and small classifiers for detecting slop, then outlines approaches that combine deliberate creative variation, structured brand guidance, and verification at inference time.

title: Routing LLM Inference in Production: From Engine Signals to Policy — Qianru Lao & Lu Zhang, OpenAI
AI Agents Are Just Distributed Systems Now — Salman Munaf, TikTok
summary: Salman Munaf argues that agents calling external services require distributed systems engineering. He describes agents as probabilistic coordinators whose actions need deterministic controls, including idempotency, bounded retries, authoritative state, scoped permissions, compensation and traces that support recovery.

title: World Models Need Causality, Not Pretty Pixels — Christopher Manning, Moonlake AI
summary: Christopher Manning traces AI and language-model history before presenting Moonlake AI's approach to embodied intelligence. He argues that useful world models need semantic state, causal dynamics and controllable objects to support planning. He describes reconstructing interactive simulations from images or video, generating their behavior in code, and refining them against real observations. Q&A addresses gaming, symbolic representations, physics, simulation-to-reality transfer and discovery.

title: What's New in Inference Engineering — Philip Kiely, Baseten
Where RL Will Take Search — Maximilian-David Rumpf, SID.ai

summary: In this recording, attributed by metadata to Maximilian-David Rumpf, the speaker introduces himself as SID.ai's founder and CEO and argues for reinforcement-learning-trained search sub-agents. He reports that agentic search is roughly twice as likely to find the right documents as classical search, but costs 100–1,000 times more and consumes 30–50% of an agent's tokens. Classical pipelines have fixed compute budgets and cannot retry when their reranker detects inadequate results. His proposed alternative learns to search, inspect documents, adjust metadata filters and iterate before returning ranked results. Search offers verifiable document-level rewards and high-throughput training opportunities; he reports improving quality with compute and incorporating latency rewards. For SID-1, he claims approximately 20-fold faster search and 100-fold lower cost than a frontier model on the presented task, citing about five seconds versus two minutes, while acknowledging that classical vector-and-reranker pipelines remain faster. Delegating retrieval also keeps irrelevant intermediate results out of the main agent's context. He forecasts applications in voice, e-commerce and private enterprise knowledge; these forecasts and benchmark claims are presented as the speaker's assertions.

title: Modality Misalignment and Originality Attribution in Short-Form Video — Aditya Gautam, Meta
summary: Aditya Gautam describes a system for detecting unexpected content changes within short-form videos and identifying copied or transformed content for attribution. The presentation divides perception, retrieval, and review among three agents powered by specialized small vision-language models, then discusses domain-specific training, human review, evaluation, and optimizations for large-scale processing.

title: 5 Voice Agent Failure Modes You'll Hit in Week One — Venky B, Plivo
summary: Venky B discusses how voice agents fail when moving from demos to production. He recommends balancing latency, cost and model capability; cleaning unreliable transcripts; collecting data through typed, validated fields with field-level evaluations; and normalizing model output before speech synthesis. Turn detection and interruption handling receive only brief closing coverage.
